explainers.title: Hello again, and welcome to Collaboration
explainers.body:
Hello, and welcome back to Global Perspectives at Ehel Academy. So far this year, most of your thinking skills have been about your own work: what you find out and what you think. This unit is different, and rather exciting, because it is all about working with other people. The skill is called Collaboration, and it is one of the most useful skills you will ever learn.

Here are all six thinking skills again, so you can see where this unit fits:

This unit is all about the fifth skill: Collaboration. Almost nothing big in the world is made by one person alone. A busy market in Hargeisa, a fishing boat landing its catch at Berbera, a family meal, a clean schoolyard: all of these need people working together. When you work well in a team, you can do things that would be far too big to do alone.

Think about the grown-ups around you. Market traders in Mogadishu, nurses caring for the ill, neighbours clearing a street after the rains: they all share a goal, share out the jobs, and solve problems together. All across the Horn of Africa, the biggest things are built by teams. A child who learns to collaborate now will be a better friend and teammate for life. That is why we teach it on purpose.
bullets: Research — finding out about the world in a careful way.
Analysis — looking closely at a topic and asking why things happen.
Evaluation — deciding how good, useful or trustworthy something is.
Reflection — thinking about how you learn and how you change your mind.
Collaboration — working well together with other people to reach a shared goal.
Communication — sharing your ideas so others understand.

explainers.title: So what is collaboration?
explainers.body:
Here is a simple meaning you can keep: collaboration means working together as a team to reach a goal. That goal has a special name in this unit. We call it a shared outcome: the one result the whole team is working for. It is 'shared' because everyone on the team wants it, not just one person.

Good collaboration is really three things joined together, and this unit will teach all three:

Notice that collaboration is not just sitting in the same room as other people. Four children sitting together, each doing their own thing, are not collaborating. A team is collaborating when they share one goal, share the work, and help each other reach it. That is the skill you will build.
bullets: Working for a shared goal — agreeing what your team is trying to do, so everyone pulls the same way.
Sharing out the jobs fairly — deciding who does what, so everyone helps and no one does everything.
Helping each other — sharing ideas, listening, and sorting out problems kindly when they come up.

explainers.title: How you will learn this unit
explainers.body:
You might be wondering something clever: how can I learn teamwork when I study at my own speed, on my own? That is a very good question, and the answer is the heart of this unit. You will plan and practise on your own with your AI tutor, and then do the real teamwork with your group in your teacher sessions. Four kinds of help work together:

So the pattern all the way through this unit is simple, and you will see it again and again: plan and practise with your AI tutor now, then do the real teamwork with your group in your next teacher session. In the old way of this subject, a book would say 'talk to your group' or 'work with your team'. In our way, you get ready with your tutor first, so that when you meet your team you are ready to do your best.
bullets: You, at your own speed. You read, think and get your part ready in your own time. You can go slowly on a hard idea, or quickly on an easy one.

Your AI tutor, ready any time, day or night. Your tutor is your planning and practice partner. With it you can plan a goal, share out the jobs, practise being a good leader, and try out what to say when people do not agree — all before you meet your team.
Your teacher sessions, about twice a week. This is where the real teamwork happens. You bring the plans you got ready, and carry them out together with your group of classmates.
Your family and community. The people at home are a real team too. You can practise sharing jobs, listening and being kind with them any day of the week.

explainers.title: Meet Layla and her team
explainers.body:
To make each skill clear, we will follow one small team of Year 4 learners all the way through the unit. They are four friends at Ehel Academy in Hargeisa: Layla, Omar, Amara and Idris. They take turns being the leader, because in a good team everyone matters and everyone gets a turn to shine.

A clever team knows what each person is good at, so the jobs can be shared out well. Here is what each of them brings:

As you meet each new collaboration skill, you will see what Layla's team does with it. By the end, they will have run a real project together, and you will do the same with your own group in your teacher sessions.

headers: A strength they bring to the team
rows: Careful and organised. Good at planning, keeping the team on track, and writing things clearly.
Friendly and chatty. Good at talking to people, asking questions, and speaking in front of others. He also loves to sing.
Creative. Good at drawing, designing and making colourful posters and maps.
Good with numbers. Enjoys sorting answers into neat tables, charts and pictograms.

explainers.title: Your Challenge: How healthy is your diet?
explainers.body:
This unit builds one big project we call your Challenge. A Challenge is a topic that matters in the wider world and also right where you live. Your Challenge this unit is a question: How healthy is your diet? Your 'diet' just means all the food and drink you have. This topic is part of a big idea called health and wellbeing.

Layla's team chose one part of that question to work on together: where do our vegetables come from, and how can we all eat well? They noticed that some vegetables travel a very long way, while others grow right here. Their shared outcome became one clear sentence: *we will find out where our vegetables come from, and help more families eat healthy, local food.*

You cannot answer a question like that by guessing. A team has to find things out, share the jobs, and put their answers together. Here are some of the jobs Layla's team will share out:

You do not have to copy this exact project. Any shared team goal about healthy food will work, such as growing vegetables at home or a healthy-snacks poster. What matters is that it is a shared outcome your group can reach together.
bullets: Agree a set of research questions about vegetables and healthy food.
Find out where people buy their vegetables, and which ones grow nearby.
Ask the school cook, and ask local farmers or market sellers, where the food comes from.
Find out which vegetables are in season, and when.
Put their answers together and plan a presentation to share what they found.
Give the presentation with a friendly message: eat local vegetables for a healthy future.

explainers.title: Three steps of collaboration this year
explainers.body:
Your collaboration skills will grow in three steps this year, like a young tree. First you are starting the skill. Then you are developing it. Then you are getting better at it. Here is what each step is really about:

Do not worry if the first tries feel tricky. Starting is meant to feel like a first try. Each skill below will move you a little further along.
bullets: Starting — working well with your team to reach your goal, and deciding what job each person will do.
Developing — sharing helpful ideas, being a fair leader, and giving each person a job that matches their skill.
Getting better — doing your own job well to help the team, and planning a shared presentation together.

explainers.title: Working together for a shared goal
explainers.body:
Every strong team begins the same way: by agreeing its shared goal. This is the one result everyone is working for, said so clearly that every person on the team could repeat it in a single sentence. Without it, four people can work hard all day and still pull in four different directions.

A good shared goal is clear (everyone understands it the same way), shared (the whole team wants it), and reachable (the team really could get there together). Often a team starts by agreeing a few research questions too, so everyone knows what to find out.

explainers.title: Deciding together, even when you do not agree
explainers.body:
A team has to make lots of decisions: which questions to ask, which jobs to do first, what to put on a poster. Sometimes everyone agrees quickly. But sometimes people disagree, and that is completely normal. A disagreement is not a fight. What matters is not whether you disagree, but how your team decides in a fair way.

Here is a friendly way for a group to decide when people do not agree. First, listen to each idea without interrupting. Second, find what you agree on, because there is almost always something. Third, choose together, perhaps by taking a vote, or by finding a middle way that takes a little from each idea. Then everyone agrees and moves on, with no one feeling like the loser.

explainers.title: Sharing out the jobs fairly
explainers.body:
A shared goal usually needs many jobs done. A team that shares the jobs fairly works far better than one where a single person does everything while the rest watch. To share fairly means everyone has a reasonable share to do, so the whole team feels useful and no one is left with too much.

Part of sharing fairly is deciding when a job is better done together and when it is better done alone. Some jobs, like carrying a heavy box or planning the whole project, are easier with two or more people. Other jobs, like drawing one poster, are fine for one person. A clever team asks, for each job: is this a together job, or an alone job?

explainers.title: Being a good leader
explainers.body:
Sometimes a team chooses a leader to help it work smoothly. A leader can be a good thing: decisions get made more quickly, and everyone knows what to do. But a bossy leader can be a problem. If the leader decides everything alone and just gives orders, the team will not feel excited, and people who disagree may not do their best.

So what does a good leader do? A good leader gives everyone a chance to speak, and listens carefully to their ideas. A good leader helps the team decide together, instead of deciding everything alone. In Layla's team, they take turns being leader, so everyone learns how it feels.

explainers.title: Sharing ideas to plan a presentation
explainers.body:
Once a team has gathered its answers, called its data, it needs to present them, which means sharing what it found with other people. A team gets the best result when everyone suggests ideas for how to do it. The clever part is not just giving your own idea, but adding to other people's ideas to make them even better.

There are many ways to present. Layla's team thought of a world map to show how far vegetables travel, a poster to show how to grow vegetables at home, a pictogram to show the best vegetables each month, and an interview with the school cook about what the school buys. A good team asks, for each idea: which needs the most work to get ready, and which needs the least?

explainers.title: Giving each person the right job for their skill
explainers.body:
When a team divides the presentation jobs, the clever trick is to match each job to a person's skill. A skill is something you are good at. When people do jobs that suit them, the work is better and everyone enjoys it more. It still needs to be fair, so everyone has a reasonable share.

Here is how different jobs match different skills:
bullets: A facts report suits a strong writer.
A poster with pictures suits a good drawer or designer.
A chart or graph of numbers suits someone good at maths.
A song to help people remember suits someone good at music.

explainers.title: Using skills and what people have done before
explainers.body:
As you get better at teamwork, you can share jobs even more cleverly. You look at two things: a person's skills (what they are good at) and their prior experience (what they have done before). If someone has already done something like a job, they can help the team even more, and they can help others learn.

Sometimes the best plan is to put people in pairs, so a job gets two sets of skills. You choose the pair whose skills and experience fit the job best.

explainers.title: Learning a new skill together
explainers.body:
A great team does not only use the skills it already has. It also helps each person learn a new skill. When you try a job you have never done before, with your team to help you, you grow. That is one of the best things about working together.

Layla's team took on a second project to practise this: a presentation for younger children about kids who miss out on school. This is part of a big topic called education for all. It had two extra challenges: the audience was younger, so the team kept things simple and fun, and each person planned to learn one new skill, not only use an old one.

explainers.title: How collaboration helps the other five skills
explainers.body:
Collaboration does not work on its own. It makes every other Global Perspectives skill stronger, and they make it stronger too.

So the teamwork you practise now will lift all your other skills too.
bullets: Research gets easier, because a team can share out the finding-out and gather far more than one person could.
Analysis grows, because teammates notice different causes and reasons that you might miss alone.
Evaluation improves, because a team can weigh an idea from many sides before deciding.
Reflection deepens, because you learn about yourself by noticing how you work with others.
Communication matters more than ever, because a team only works if its members share their ideas clearly.

explainers.title: Putting it all together
explainers.body: You have now met every collaboration skill in this unit. Here is how they fit together into a simple set of steps you can use for any team project:
bullets: Agree a clear shared goal the whole team wants.
Decide together fairly, even when people do not agree at first.
Share out the jobs fairly, deciding what is a together job and what is an alone job.
Choose a good leader who lets everyone speak and listens.
Share ideas for how to present, and add to each other's ideas.
Give each person a job that matches their skill and what they have done before.
Help each person learn a new skill, and share the presentation together.

explainers.title: What comes next
explainers.body: The next unit is Communication. Once you can work well in a team, communication teaches you to share your ideas and findings clearly, so that other people really understand you. Good collaboration and good communication go hand in hand: a team needs both. Well done for learning to be someone people are glad to have on their team.

bigIdeas.title: One big idea to remember
lines: In Global Perspectives, the topic is like a bus, and the skill is where the bus takes you.
In this unit our topic is food and a healthy diet, and where our vegetables come from.
But the real prize is not the food project. It is to become someone people are glad to have on their team.

bigIdeas.title: Two questions a good team keeps asking
lines: How well do I work with my team? Do I share ideas, listen, and do my fair share?
How well do we work as a team? Do we agree a goal, share the jobs fairly, and reach the best result together?
Coming back to these two questions is one of the best ways to become a stronger teammate.

bigIdeas.title: Your team project runs through everything
lines: Pick one healthy-food project you could really do with your group, such as where our vegetables come from, growing food at home, or a healthy-snacks poster.
You will build on it in every activity, so choose something your team really cares about.
By the end, you will have a real plan your team can carry out.

bigIdeas.title: Four steps to decide fairly
lines: Listen to each idea without interrupting.
Find what everyone agrees on, which is usually the same shared goal.
Choose together, by a quick vote or a middle way that takes a little from each idea.
Agree and move on, so no one feels like the loser.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Say hello to your AI tutor. Tell it: I am starting Unit 5 of Global Perspectives, and the skill is Collaboration.
Ask it: in one or two simple sentences, why is being a good teammate useful, even outside of school?
Then tell your tutor about a time you worked well in a team, and a time teamwork was hard, and why.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor about a team food project you could do, real or imagined.
Ask it to help you write your shared goal as one clear sentence, starting with the words Our shared goal is.
Then ask: is my goal clear, shared, and something a team could really reach? Ask it to help you write three research questions too.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor about a decision your team needs to make.
Ask the tutor to take a different view from you, so you can practise deciding fairly.
Practise the steps out loud: listen, find what you agree on, choose together, then agree and move on.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor about a time someone was bossy in a group, and how it felt.
Ask it for three friendly things a good leader could say to give everyone a turn to speak.
Then practise: your tutor is a quiet team member, and you, the leader, gently invite its idea.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor one idea for how your team could present its findings.
Ask the tutor to add to your idea, then you add to its idea, back and forth, three times.
Notice how the idea grows. Ask the tutor which way of presenting would need the most work, and which the least.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor the jobs your presentation needs, and the skill each one needs.
Ask it to help you match each job to the kind of person who would do it best.
Then ask: is my share fair, or does one person have too much to do?

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor about something you have done before, like a poster, a song, a chart, or a report.
Ask it: which team job would my skill and my experience suit best?
Then ask the tutor to help you pick a good partner-skill to work with yours on that job.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor about a new skill you would like to try on a team, like drawing, speaking, or making a chart.
Ask it how a teammate could help you learn that new skill while still helping the team.
Then ask the tutor for one tip on making a presentation simple and fun for younger children.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor your project and your shared goal sentence.
Ask it: is my goal clear, and is it something a team of children could really reach?
Ask the tutor to help you make your three research questions sharper and simpler.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Describe the decision to your AI tutor, and ask it to argue for a different idea than yours.
Practise the four steps out loud, all the way to choosing together.
Ask the tutor for feedback: did I listen, stay friendly, and treat the other idea fairly?

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your questions to your AI tutor.
Ask it to help you choose the best way to answer each one: survey, interview, online, or labels.
Ask the tutor to suggest one good person your team could interview about local food.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your list of jobs to your AI tutor.
Ask it: does my way of sharing the jobs look fair, or does anyone have too much?
Ask the tutor which of my jobs are better done together, and which are fine alone.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Ask your AI tutor to pretend to be a bossy leader, then talk about how it feels.
Now you be the good leader, and let the tutor play a quiet team member you invite to speak.
Ask the tutor for feedback: did I give everyone a turn and listen well?

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor your first idea for presenting.
Take turns adding to it: the tutor adds an idea, then you add to the tutor's idea, three times.
Ask the tutor which way of presenting needs the most work to get ready, and which needs the least.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your list of jobs and skills to your AI tutor.
Ask it: does each job match the right skill, and is the share fair?
Ask the tutor if any job needs a skill I have not planned for yet.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your matches to your AI tutor.
Ask it: do my matches use each person's skill and experience well?
Ask the tutor to help you pick the best pair for one job, and to explain why they fit.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your presentation plan to your AI tutor.
Ask it: are the parts in a sensible order, and does everyone have a turn?
Ask the tutor for one way to make the ending message clear and easy to remember.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor about the younger audience and the new skill you want to try.
Ask it for one tip to make your presentation simple and fun for little children.
Ask the tutor how a teammate could help you learn your new skill while still helping the team.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your three team sentences to your AI tutor.
Ask it: from what I said, what is one thing I could do to be an even better teammate?
Ask the tutor to help you plan your very next step with your group.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your fixed sentences to your AI tutor.
Ask it whether your rewrites are now fair, friendly, and clear.
Ask the tutor to show you one more way to reword any answer you found hard.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your five answers to your AI tutor.
Ask it to tell you which answer was strongest, and why.
Ask the tutor to give you one more story like these to try.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your reflection answers to your AI tutor.
Ask it to help you notice how your teamwork changed from the start of the unit to now.
Ask the tutor to suggest one collaboration skill to focus on in the next unit, and why.

speakingPrompts.title: A family touch
lines: Ask someone at home about a time they worked in a team, at work, at the market, or in the community.
Ask them: what made the team work well, and what made it hard?
Bring their answer to your next teacher session. The grown-ups around you are full of teamwork wisdom.

speakingPrompts.title: A family touch
lines: Do a small job with someone at home, such as cooking or tidying, as a team.
Give each other one job, and try to learn one new thing from them.
Afterwards, tell them one thing they did that made the teamwork go well.

teacherSessions.title: Layla's team agrees its goal
lines: Layla, Omar, Amara and Idris all cared about food, but at first each imagined a slightly different project.
So they talked, and agreed one shared goal: we will find out where our vegetables come from, and help families eat healthy, local food.
Then they agreed four research questions: Where do people buy their vegetables? Which vegetables grow in our community? Where do our vegetables come from? Which vegetables are in season, and when?
Now every job they do points at the same goal. A shared goal keeps a team pulling in one direction.

teacherSessions.title: Two ideas, one fair decision
lines: Omar wanted to research fruit, like mangoes and bananas. Amara wanted to research vegetables, like tomatoes and onions.
Instead of arguing, they listened to each other. They found what they agreed on: both wanted healthy, local food.
The team took a quick vote, and vegetables won by three to one. Omar was happy, because the team promised to add one fruit, the banana, to the map.
The decision was fair, everyone was heard, and the team moved on cheerfully.

teacherSessions.title: Layla's team shares out the finding-out
lines: Asking parents where they buy vegetables went to Omar, who is friendly and enjoys talking to people.
Looking online for where bananas and mangoes grow went to Idris, who is careful and good with facts.
Reading the labels at the shop to see where food comes from went to Amara, working with Idris, because two pairs of eyes are quicker.
Keeping the plan and the questions tidy went to Layla, who is organised. Everyone had a fair share that suited them.

teacherSessions.title: In your next teacher session
lines: Bring your list of jobs and your idea of who could do each one.
As a group, agree together who takes which job, and check the share feels fair to everyone.
This is real collaboration: you planned with your AI tutor, and now you decide together as a team.

teacherSessions.title: Layla leads, the good way
lines: It was Layla's turn to lead while the team planned the poster.
A bossy leader might say: I have decided, we will do it my way. Layla did not do that.
Instead she said: Amara, what do you think? Idris, what would you add? She listened to each idea first.
Then the team chose together. Because Layla listened, everyone felt keen to help, and the poster was better for it.

teacherSessions.title: The team builds one idea together
lines: Amara said: we could make a big poster about vegetables.
Omar added to it: even better, we could add a world map, to show how far some vegetables travel.
Idris added: and I could make a pictogram of the best vegetables each month, so families know what to buy.
Layla finished: then let us end with a friendly message — eat local vegetables for a healthy future. Each idea made the last one better.

teacherSessions.title: The team matches jobs to skills
lines: Writing the short facts report went to Layla, who writes clearly.
Making the poster and the world map went to Amara, who loves to draw and design.
Making the pictogram and counting the survey answers went to Idris, who is good with numbers.
Doing the interview and singing a little healthy-food song went to Omar, who is chatty and loves to sing. Every job matched a skill, and the share was fair.

teacherSessions.title: Choosing the best pair for each job
lines: Grace had sung in a school concert before, so she was a great choice for the song.
Amara had made a poster for sports day, so she and a partner made the slogan and a colourful sticker.
Idris had made a chart of rubbish collected on a clean-up, so he made the vegetable chart with a partner.
Layla had written a report for science club, so she led the facts report. The team used both skills and past experience to pick each pair.

teacherSessions.title: The team plans to learn something new
lines: Idris, who is good with numbers, chose to try speaking at the front for the first time.
Omar, who loves talking, chose to try drawing a simple picture story for the little ones.
Amara chose to make her very first pictogram, with Idris to help her.
Because they helped each other, each person did their job and learned a new skill at the same time.

teacherSessions.title: In your next teacher session
lines: Bring the plan you made with your AI tutor, with a job for every person.
As a group, agree the jobs, and let each person choose one new skill they would like to try.
Then help each other. That is what a real team is for.

teacherSessions.title: The team's whole journey, from question to presentation
lines: They agreed a shared goal: find out where our vegetables come from, and help families eat well.
They decided together, shared out the finding-out, and took turns being a fair leader.
They shared ideas for a poster, a world map, a pictogram and an interview, and matched each job to a skill.
They each learned a new skill, gave their presentation, and ended with their message: eat local vegetables for a healthy future.
Four friends turned one good question into a real project that helped their whole school.
In the Activities file, you will run these same steps on your own project, planning with your AI tutor and carrying it out with your group.

teacherSessions.title: In your next teacher session
lines: Share your shared goal and your questions with your group.
Together, agree on one shared goal you all want, in a single sentence everyone could repeat.

teacherSessions.title: In your next teacher session
lines: When a real decision comes up in your group, use the same four steps.
Notice how much easier it is to decide, now that you have practised.

teacherSessions.title: A model match
lines: Question: Where do families buy their vegetables? Best way: a short survey of parents and carers.
Question: Where do our bananas grow? Best way: search online, and read the labels at the shop.
Question: What does the school buy, and from where? Best way: an interview with the school cook.
Fill in a table like this for your own questions.

teacherSessions.title: A model row
lines: Job: ask parents where they buy vegetables. Who: a friendly, chatty person. Together or alone: alone is fine, but two can ask more people.
Job: plan the whole poster. Who: the whole team. Together or alone: together, because it needs everyone's ideas.

teacherSessions.title: In your next teacher session
lines: Bring your job list. As a group, agree who takes each job.
Check together that the share feels fair, and that everyone has something to do.

teacherSessions.title: A good leader and a bossy leader
lines: A good leader says: Idris, what do you think? Let us decide together.
A bossy leader says: I have decided, we will do it my way. Do not argue.
The good leader's team feels keen to help. The bossy leader's team does not do its best.

teacherSessions.title: A model of building on an idea
lines: We could make a poster about vegetables.
Even better, we could add a world map to show how far some vegetables travel.
And we could also make a pictogram of the best vegetables each month, and end with the message: eat local vegetables for a healthy future.

teacherSessions.title: A model match of job to skill
lines: A facts report needs a strong writer.
A poster with pictures needs a good drawer or designer.
A chart of numbers needs someone good at maths.
A song to help people remember needs someone good at music.
Fill in a table like this for your own presentation.

teacherSessions.title: In your next teacher session
lines: Bring your job-and-skill table. As a group, agree who takes each job.
Check that each job matches someone's skill, and that everyone has a fair share.

teacherSessions.title: A model plan
lines: 1. Welcome and our question — Omar.
2. The world map: how far vegetables travel — Amara.
3. The pictogram: the best vegetables each month — Idris.
4. Our message and a short song: eat local vegetables for a healthy future — the whole team.

teacherSessions.title: In your next teacher session
lines: Agree your presentation plan with your group, and give everyone a part.
Practise it once together, then decide what to make even better before you present it.

toolkit.title: The collaboration steps at a glance
toolkit.intro: Whatever your team project, good teamwork follows the same steps. Come back to this list whenever you feel stuck.
items: Agree a shared goal: the one result the whole team wants.
Decide together: fairly, even when people do not agree at first.
Share out the jobs: fairly, deciding what is a together job and what is an alone job.
Choose a good leader: one who lets everyone speak and listens.
Share ideas: for how to present, and add to each other's ideas.
Match jobs to skills: and to what people have done before.
Help each other learn, and share the presentation together.

toolkit.title: What is collaboration?
toolkit.intro:
Collaboration means working together as a team to reach a goal, called a shared outcome. It is not just being in the same room. A team is collaborating when they share one goal, share out the work fairly, and help each other reach it.

Two habits sit at the heart of it. First, share ideas and listen, so the team's thinking is better than any one person's. Second, work fairly and kindly, so everyone feels useful and problems get sorted out gently. If you remember nothing else, remember those two habits.

toolkit.title: Your Stage 4 Collaboration learning goals
toolkit.intro: Your collaboration skills grow in three steps this year. Here are the real learning goals for each step, in simple words. Your teacher may talk about these.

toolkit.title: Sentence starters for sharing and building on ideas
toolkit.intro: Use these to add your own ideas, and to grow other people's ideas instead of blocking them.
items: I have an idea: we could ...
What if we tried ...?
Even better, we could ...
Building on that, we could also ...
Yes, and we could add ...
That gives me an idea: what about ...?

toolkit.title: Sentence starters for listening and encouraging others
toolkit.intro: Use these to make sure everyone is heard, especially the quieter members of your team.
items: So you mean we could ...? (to show you listened)
That is a good start, tell us more.
You are good at this, what do you think?
We have not heard from you yet, would you like to share?
I like that idea because ...
Thank you, that really helps the team.

toolkit.title: How we will divide the work fairly
toolkit.intro: Share the jobs so everyone has a fair part. For each job, decide who does it, and whether it is better done together or alone. Copy this table to plan the sharing.

toolkit.title: A good leader does and does not
toolkit.intro: A good leader helps the team without being bossy. Use this as a checklist.

toolkit.title: A good leader does ...
items: gives everyone a chance to speak.
listens carefully to each idea.
helps the team decide together.
thanks people and keeps the team cheerful.

toolkit.title: A good leader does not ...
items: decide everything alone.
give orders without listening.
leave anyone out, or let one person do everything.
ignore a quiet person's idea.

toolkit.title: Match the job to the skill
toolkit.intro: Give each job to the person whose skill fits it best, while keeping the share fair. Here are some jobs and the skills they need.

rows: A poster or a map with pictures
A song to help people remember
An interview or a talk to a group
Keeping the plan and the time tidy

toolkit.title: Deciding together when the team does not agree
toolkit.intro:
Disagreeing is normal. What matters is deciding in a fair way. Follow these four steps.

Keep your voice friendly and kind. You are choosing the best idea for the team, not trying to win.
items: Listen to each idea, letting each person finish without being interrupted.
Find what you agree on, which is almost always the same shared goal.
Choose together, by a quick vote or a middle way that takes a little from each idea.
Agree and move on, so no one feels like the loser.

toolkit.title: A good team member and a good team
toolkit.intro: Use these as a checklist for how to behave in a team.

toolkit.title: A good team member ...
items: always listens, does a fair share, and helps others.
always shares ideas and adds to other people's.
never puts a teammate down or takes over every job.

toolkit.title: A good team ...
items: always agrees a shared goal and shares the work fairly.
always decides fairly and helps each person learn.
never leaves one person to do everything, or ignores a quiet voice.

toolkit.title: Making the most of your teacher sessions
toolkit.intro: Remember the pattern of this unit: plan and practise with your AI tutor, then do the real teamwork with your group in your teacher sessions. Here is how to make each session count.
items: Come ready: bring the plan or the job list you made with your AI tutor.
Start by agreeing your shared goal, and what you want to finish this session.
Share out the jobs quickly, using each person's skill, so no time is wasted.
Listen to everyone, and check the quieter members have had their say.
Near the end, agree who does what before next time.

activities.title: Choose your project and your shared goal
activities.label: Activity 1: Choose your project and your shared goal
activities.intro: Every team starts by agreeing what it is working for. First choose a project, then write your shared goal: the one result the whole team wants, in a single clear sentence. A good shared goal is small enough to reach, but big enough to be worth doing.
steps: Write the project you will work on: 'Our team project is ...'.
Write your shared goal in one sentence: 'Our shared goal is ...'.
Write three research questions your team could answer, such as: Where do people buy their vegetables?

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor your project and your shared goal sentence.
Ask it: is my goal clear, and is it something a team of children could really reach?
Ask the tutor to help you make your three research questions sharper and simpler.

boxes.title: In your next teacher session
lines: Share your shared goal and your questions with your group.
Together, agree on one shared goal you all want, in a single sentence everyone could repeat.

activities.title: Decide together when you do not agree
activities.label: Activity 2: Decide together when you do not agree
activities.intro: Teams do not always agree straight away, and that is fine. Here you practise deciding in a fair way. The trick is to listen first, find what you agree on, then choose together by voting or by a middle way.
steps: Think of a decision your team must make, such as which food to research or what to put first on a poster.
Write two different ideas fairly, as if you liked both.
Write one thing both ideas agree on, and one fair way to choose between them.

boxes.title: Four steps to decide fairly
lines: Listen to each idea without interrupting.
Find what everyone agrees on, which is usually the same shared goal.
Choose together, by a quick vote or a middle way that takes a little from each idea.
Agree and move on, so no one feels like the loser.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Describe the decision to your AI tutor, and ask it to argue for a different idea than yours.
Practise the four steps out loud, all the way to choosing together.
Ask the tutor for feedback: did I listen, stay friendly, and treat the other idea fairly?

boxes.title: In your next teacher session
lines: When a real decision comes up in your group, use the same four steps.
Notice how much easier it is to decide, now that you have practised.

activities.title: Match each question to a way of finding the answer
activities.label: Activity 3: Match each question to a way of finding the answer
activities.intro: A team has to decide how to answer each question. There are many ways: a survey of parents and carers, an interview with an adult like the school cook or a local farmer, a search online, or reading the labels on food at the shop. Match each question to the best way to find the answer.

headers: How we will find the answer

boxes.title: A model match
lines: Question: Where do families buy their vegetables? Best way: a short survey of parents and carers.
Question: Where do our bananas grow? Best way: search online, and read the labels at the shop.
Question: What does the school buy, and from where? Best way: an interview with the school cook.
Fill in a table like this for your own questions.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your questions to your AI tutor.
Ask it to help you choose the best way to answer each one: survey, interview, online, or labels.
Ask the tutor to suggest one good person your team could interview about local food.

activities.title: Share out the jobs fairly
activities.label: Activity 4: Share out the jobs fairly
activities.intro: Now share the jobs so everyone has a fair part. For each job, decide who does it, and whether it is a together job or an alone job.
steps: List at least five jobs your project needs done.
Next to each job, write who could do it, and why.
In the last column, write 'together' or 'alone', and say why.

boxes.title: A model row
lines: Job: ask parents where they buy vegetables. Who: a friendly, chatty person. Together or alone: alone is fine, but two can ask more people.
Job: plan the whole poster. Who: the whole team. Together or alone: together, because it needs everyone's ideas.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your list of jobs to your AI tutor.
Ask it: does my way of sharing the jobs look fair, or does anyone have too much?
Ask the tutor which of my jobs are better done together, and which are fine alone.

boxes.title: In your next teacher session
lines: Bring your job list. As a group, agree who takes each job.
Check together that the share feels fair, and that everyone has something to do.

activities.title: Be a good leader
activities.label: Activity 5: Be a good leader
activities.intro: A good leader helps a team without being bossy. Here you think about what a good leader does, and what a good leader should never do.
steps: Write two things a good leader does, such as: gives everyone a chance to speak.
Write two things a good leader should not do, such as: decide everything alone.
Write one friendly sentence a leader could say to invite a quiet person to share an idea.

boxes.title: A good leader and a bossy leader
lines: A good leader says: Idris, what do you think? Let us decide together.
A bossy leader says: I have decided, we will do it my way. Do not argue.
The good leader's team feels keen to help. The bossy leader's team does not do its best.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Ask your AI tutor to pretend to be a bossy leader, then talk about how it feels.
Now you be the good leader, and let the tutor play a quiet team member you invite to speak.
Ask the tutor for feedback: did I give everyone a turn and listen well?

activities.title: Choose how to present your findings
activities.label: Activity 6: Choose how to present your findings
activities.intro: When your team has its answers, it needs to present them. Practise sharing ideas and adding to each other's ideas. Then think about which way of presenting needs the most work, and which needs the least.
steps: Write one idea for how to present, starting with 'We could ...'.
Now add to it twice, as if you were a teammate: 'Even better, we could ...' and 'And we could also ...'.
List these four ways to present, and mark which needs the most work and which the least: a world map, a poster, a pictogram, an interview.

boxes.title: A model of building on an idea
lines: We could make a poster about vegetables.
Even better, we could add a world map to show how far some vegetables travel.
And we could also make a pictogram of the best vegetables each month, and end with the message: eat local vegetables for a healthy future.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor your first idea for presenting.
Take turns adding to it: the tutor adds an idea, then you add to the tutor's idea, three times.
Ask the tutor which way of presenting needs the most work to get ready, and which needs the least.

activities.title: Match each job to the right skill
activities.label: Activity 7: Match each job to the right skill
activities.intro: A team works best when each job matches a person's skill. Match the presentation jobs to the skills they need, so your team can share the work fairly and well.

headers: Who could do it, and why

boxes.title: A model match of job to skill
lines: A facts report needs a strong writer.
A poster with pictures needs a good drawer or designer.
A chart of numbers needs someone good at maths.
A song to help people remember needs someone good at music.
Fill in a table like this for your own presentation.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your list of jobs and skills to your AI tutor.
Ask it: does each job match the right skill, and is the share fair?
Ask the tutor if any job needs a skill I have not planned for yet.

boxes.title: In your next teacher session
lines: Bring your job-and-skill table. As a group, agree who takes each job.
Check that each job matches someone's skill, and that everyone has a fair share.

activities.title: Skills, experience, and the best pair
activities.label: Activity 8: Skills, experience, and the best pair
activities.intro:
Now share jobs even more cleverly, using both skills (what people are good at) and prior experience (what they have done before). Sometimes two people make the best team for a job.

Here are four classmates and what they have done before. Match each one to the job that suits them best, then choose a good pair for each job.
steps: Match each person to the job that fits their experience: a song, a slogan and sticker, a facts report, or a number chart.
For one job, choose a good pair of people to work together, and say why.
Write one job where you would like to learn a new skill yourself.

rows: Sang in a school concert last year.
Made a bright poster for sports day.
Made a chart of the rubbish collected on a clean-up.
Wrote a report for science club.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your matches to your AI tutor.
Ask it: do my matches use each person's skill and experience well?
Ask the tutor to help you pick the best pair for one job, and to explain why they fit.

activities.title: Plan your shared presentation
activities.label: Activity 9: Plan your shared presentation
activities.intro: Now put your project together into a presentation plan. Decide the order of the parts, and who presents each one. End with a friendly message, such as: eat local vegetables for a healthy future.
steps: Write your team's shared goal at the top.
Fill in the plan below with at least four parts, in a sensible order.
For each part, write who presents it, and check that everyone has a turn.

boxes.title: A model plan
lines: 1. Welcome and our question — Omar.
2. The world map: how far vegetables travel — Amara.
3. The pictogram: the best vegetables each month — Idris.
4. Our message and a short song: eat local vegetables for a healthy future — the whole team.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your presentation plan to your AI tutor.
Ask it: are the parts in a sensible order, and does everyone have a turn?
Ask the tutor for one way to make the ending message clear and easy to remember.

boxes.title: In your next teacher session
lines: Agree your presentation plan with your group, and give everyone a part.
Practise it once together, then decide what to make even better before you present it.

activities.title: Plan for a younger audience, and learn a new skill
activities.label: Activity 10: Plan for a younger audience, and learn a new skill
activities.intro: For your last activity, plan a short presentation for younger children about kids who miss out on school. This has two extra challenges: keep it simple and fun for little ones, and plan to learn one new skill, not only use an old one.
steps: Write one way to make your presentation simple and fun for younger children.
Write one new skill you would like to try, such as speaking at the front, drawing, or making a chart.
Write who could help you learn that new skill, and how.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor about the younger audience and the new skill you want to try.
Ask it for one tip to make your presentation simple and fun for little children.
Ask the tutor how a teammate could help you learn your new skill while still helping the team.

boxes.title: A family touch
lines: Do a small job with someone at home, such as cooking or tidying, as a team.
Give each other one job, and try to learn one new thing from them.
Afterwards, tell them one thing they did that made the teamwork go well.

activities.title: Your team checkpoint
activities.label: Your team checkpoint
activities.intro:
You have now planned a real team project. Pull it together by finishing these three sentences about your teamwork, in your own words:

Keep this checkpoint safe. You will look back at it during Reflection, and it will show you how much your collaboration has grown.
steps: Our team worked best when ...
One thing we found hard was ...
Next time, our team will ...

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your three team sentences to your AI tutor.
Ask it: from what I said, what is one thing I could do to be an even better teammate?
Ask the tutor to help you plan your very next step with your group.

practice.intro: Answer these in your notebook or out loud with your AI tutor. There are 12 questions. Do not worry if some are tricky; that is how you find out what to practise next. Give your own words rather than copying from the other files.
practice.prompt: In your own words, what does collaboration mean?
practice.answer: Collaboration means working together as a team to reach a shared goal. (Any answer with this idea is correct.)

practice.prompt: The one result a whole team is working for is called the shared ______.
practice.answer: Outcome (the shared outcome).

practice.prompt: True or false: a team is any group of children sitting in the same room.
practice.answer: False. A team is only collaborating when they share one goal, share the work, and help each other.

practice.prompt: When your team does not agree, name one good thing to do first.
practice.answer: Listen to each idea without interrupting. (Also correct: find what everyone agrees on.)

practice.prompt: When you share out the jobs, you should share them ______, so no one has too much.
practice.answer: Fairly (so everyone has a reasonable share and no one has too much).

practice.prompt: Give one example of a job that is better done together, and one that is fine to do alone.
practice.answer: Together job: planning the whole project, or carrying something heavy. Alone job: drawing one poster, or reading labels. (Any sensible example.)

practice.prompt: Name one thing a good leader does.
practice.answer: Any one of: gives everyone a chance to speak, listens carefully, helps the team decide together.

practice.prompt: Name one thing a good leader should not do.
practice.answer: Any one of: decides everything alone, just gives orders, does not listen to the team.

practice.prompt: Name two ways to present what your team found out.
practice.answer: Any two of: a world map, a poster, a pictogram, an interview, a chart, a song.

practice.prompt: Match a job to a skill: who should make a chart of numbers?
practice.answer: Someone who is good at maths.

practice.prompt: Prior experience means the things you have ______ before.
practice.answer: Done (the things you have done before).

practice.prompt: Name one good reason for a team to help each person learn a new skill.
practice.answer: Any sensible reason, such as: everyone gets better, the team can do more next time, and it is fun to learn together.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.intro: Match each collaboration word (1 to 6) to the correct meaning (A to F). Write the pairs, such as 1-C.
practice.prompt: Shared outcome
options: A. To share the jobs out between the team members.
B. The one result the whole team is working for.
C. The things a person is good at.
D. A person who helps a team decide and gives everyone a turn.
E. Sharing what your team found out with other people.
F. The things you have already done before.
practice.answer: B — The one result the whole team is working for.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Divide
practice.answer: A — To share the jobs out between the team members.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Leader
practice.answer: D — A person who helps a team decide and gives everyone a turn.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Skills
practice.answer: C — The things a person is good at.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Prior experience
practice.answer: F — The things you have already done before.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Presentation
practice.answer: E — Sharing what your team found out with other people.

practice.intro: These short stories ask you to use what you have learned. Write a sentence or two for each.
practice.prompt: Two teammates want to research different foods. How could the team decide in a fair way?
practice.answer: The team could listen to both ideas, find what they agree on, then take a quick vote or find a middle way, such as researching one of each.

practice.prompt: Amara has drawn a lovely poster, but Idris has been given six jobs and Omar has none. How could the team make the share fair?
practice.answer: The team should share the jobs again, so Omar has some jobs and Idris does not have too many. A fair share means everyone helps.

practice.prompt: Layla is the leader today, but she wants to decide everything alone. What should she do instead?
practice.answer: Layla should give everyone a chance to speak, listen to their ideas, and help the team decide together, instead of deciding alone.

practice.prompt: The team needs a chart of numbers, a song, and a facts report. Who should do each one, and why?
practice.answer: The chart goes to someone good at maths, the song to someone good at music, and the report to a strong writer. Each job matches a skill.

practice.prompt: Idris has never spoken at the front before, but he would like to try. How could the team help him learn this new skill?
practice.answer: The team could pair Idris with a confident speaker, let him practise a small part first, and cheer him on, so he learns the new skill safely.

reflection.prompt: Working on my own, at my own speed ...
Planning and practising with my AI tutor before I met my team ...
Doing the real teamwork with my group in our teacher sessions ...
Practising teamwork with my family or neighbours ...

mistakes: Starting the work before agreeing a clear shared goal.
One person doing every job while the others watch.
Blocking ideas instead of adding to them.
Forgetting the quiet members, so their good ideas are never heard.
A bossy leader deciding everything alone.
Letting a disagreement turn into a fight instead of deciding fairly.

selfAssessment.statement: I can work well with my team to reach our goal.
I can agree a clear shared goal with my team.
I can help my team decide fairly, even when we do not agree.
I can help share out the jobs fairly.
I can say what job each person will do to reach our goal.
I can be a good leader who lets everyone speak and listens.
I can share ideas that help my team, and add to others' ideas.
I can match a job to the right person's skill.
I can use skills and prior experience to pick a good pair.
I can help plan and share a presentation with my team.
I can try to learn a new skill to help my team.
